title: Large independent sets in three-colorable graphs
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: An exposition of OpenAI's proof (2026) that for every delta > 0 it is NP-hard to tell graphs with a proper coloring by three colors from graphs in which every independent set has fewer than delta |V| vertices, from two theorems of the literature that are named hypotheses and are not proved here: the PCP theorem and the parallel repetition theorem (through the Label Cover instances of the course on 2-to-1 games). A third theorem that the proof uses, T. Austin's theorem that a function on a cube that is Lipschitz for the sup distance is close to a function of a bounded number of coordinates, is proved in the course 'Hypercontractivity on a torus and juntas for Lipschitz functions'. The first lesson constructs the graph from a Label Cover instance (layers of tuples of questions, families of phases, links of length 0 along the tests, the half shift, vertices as the outcomes of a random experiment) and proves the three-coloring when all tests can be satisfied. The second lesson proves the tools on Lipschitz functions: extension from a finite set, the decomposition of a function by means over coordinates, and two bounds on influences that do not depend on the number of coordinates. The third lesson turns an independent set into Lipschitz functions and bounded lists of answers, and proves that the lists of separated sets of layers are disjoint with high probability when the value of the instance is small. The fourth and fifth lessons prove the alignment theorem for such families of lists, with complete proofs of the minimax theorem and of Ramsey's theorem and with a random pattern on the rational numbers whose law depends only on the order. The sixth lesson proves the bound for the density of an independent set at an aligned pair, gives the order in which the numbers of the construction are chosen, and proves the theorem.
prerequisites: the lesson 'Projection games and the base game' of the course 'Two-to-one games with perfect completeness' (Theorem 5.1 there, from the named hypotheses (PCP) and (PR))
core course Measure and Integration (D10): the Lebesgue integral on a cube, Fubini's theorem, countable additivity of the Lebesgue measure on [0,1)
finite probability; compact sets in R^n
the lesson 'Lipschitz functions are close to juntas' of the course 'Hypercontractivity on a torus and juntas for Lipschitz functions' (Theorem 4.1 there is Theorem (J) of the second lesson)
the lessons prove every other fact they use

checks.reading: The manuscript 'Hardness of finding large independent sets in three-colorable graphs' (OpenAI, 24 Sep 2026, in the revision of the repository on 13 Oct 2026; eight sections, about 69 KB of TeX) was read in full on 13 Oct 2026, and every step of its own argument was derived again while the six lessons were written: the construction and the three-coloring; the two bounds on influences from the junta theorem; the function of an independent set, its odd Lipschitz extensions and their compatibility along a chain; the lists of a set of layers and the bound d^2 sigma for separated sets; the alignment lemma (patterns, minimax, Ramsey homogenization, consistent limit laws, the random array on the rationals, the cut and its invariance, the rational law); the coefficient test (auxiliary phases, layers with coefficient 0, layers with positive coefficient, mean square, absorption of the phases, discretization); the order of the constants and the final count 6 eps + 2 eps. No error found. The external junta theorem was compared with T. Austin, 'On the failure of concentration for the l-infinity ball' (arXiv:1309.3315v4, Theorem 1.1 and Section 2, read on 13 Oct 2026): the manuscript quotes it correctly and its passage from the L^1 bound to the L^2 bound is correct. The theorem itself was NOT checked. The Label Cover input is Theorem 5.1 of the first lesson of the course on 2-to-1 games, from the hypotheses (PCP) and (PR), which were not checked either. Differences of presentation, none a correction: the compatibility bound is proved as 64/D (rounding to a nearest grid point), where the manuscript states 2L/D = 128/D, so the condition (P5) of the course is 64/D < gamma; the lists are defined for a 'datum' (a tuple and maps), which makes the locality used in the separated-lists lemma explicit; the random array on the rationals is realized on [0,1) with the Lebesgue measure by nested intervals, its axioms hold for every sample point, and the invariance of the law of the cut is proved from the finite laws through decreasing limits, without a uniqueness theorem for measures on infinite products; the minimax theorem and Ramsey's theorem are proved in full; the preprocessing of degenerate formulas is replaced by the form of the hypothesis (PCP) of the course on 2-to-1 games. Own additions: for s = 2 no set is bad; for s = 3 the explicit law uniform on the sets {1,b,r} has bad probability at most d/(r-2) (Proposition 1.6 of the fourth lesson), and for d = 1, r = 4 this is the value of the game (Exercise 6.1). Checked by the programs plan/checks_20261013/is_check_reduction.py (link distance by shortest paths in exact arithmetic for three small instances with r = 2: T is an isometry, the first branch occurs for an instance of value 1/2 and not for two instances of value 1, the evaluation map does not increase distances, the edge rule is symmetric, the three-coloring is proper on all 73,728 outcomes; the function f of a color class is odd, 1 on A, constant across the links of length 0; the extension F is odd, 64-Lipschitz and agrees with f on the grid), is_check_analysis.py (the decomposition and the influences on a finite model; the identity of the coefficient test and the absorption of the phases in exact arithmetic for 300 random cases; the level inequality), and is_check_alignment.py (bad sets by search and by intersections; s = 2; the two witnesses for s = 3; the value of the game for s = 3, d = 1 is 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 for r = 4, 5, 6, with exact bounds from both sides). All three programs passed at their first complete run; a first version of the third program, which listed all families on 14 lists, was stopped after ten minutes as too slow and replaced by a search over witnesses. This is not a failed check. Update of 13 Oct 2026, after the first version of 02:50 UTC: the junta theorem is not a hypothesis of the course any more. It was proved in full in the new course hypercontractivity-on-a-torus-and-juntas (private commit d15df28a), in the form used here and with an explicit bound; the statement (J) of the second lesson is a theorem with a link to that proof, and the theorem of the course is proved from (PCP) and (PR) alone. The lessons 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 were changed accordingly (wording only; no change of a mathematical statement other than the removal of the hypothesis).

open_obligations: Theorem (J) of the second lesson (T. Austin) is proved in the course hypercontractivity-on-a-torus-and-juntas, for the cube with a Lipschitz condition, which is the case used here. That proof was written and checked by the same model in the same session and has not been checked by a second reader.
Named hypotheses (PCP) and (PR), through Theorem 5.1 of the lesson 'Projection games and the base game' of the course on 2-to-1 games: not proved in the programme and not checked.

The theorem of the course is an existence statement for every fixed delta: the constants of the map (r, s, m, P, lambda, mu, the answer sets) exist, and the proof gives no bound for them, because the alignment theorem is proved by contradiction (the junta theorem has an explicit bound). The manuscript's remark that r and mu can be found by a terminating search is relayed in the fifth lesson in one paragraph and not worked out.

Relayed and not checked: the statements of the manuscript's introduction about earlier and later results (hardness of coloring 3-colorable graphs with 4 and 5 colors, conditional results, the theorem of Fei, Minzer and Wang, algorithmic bounds). They are not in the lessons.
Proposition 4.2 of the first lesson (polynomial time) is proved at the level of counting the objects and naming a shortest-path algorithm; no machine model or encoding is fixed.
The lessons were written and checked by one model in one session; they have not been checked by a second reader.
